benchmark: External benchmark, usually the repo rate
reset: At least once every three months
note: Most new floating-rate retail loans must be linked to an external benchmark, and most banks use the repo rate. When the rate resets, borrowers can choose a higher EMI, a longer tenure, or both.

benchmark: Bank's marginal cost of funds based lending rate
reset: On the loan's reset date, often yearly
note: Loans priced off a bank's internal MCLR follow policy moves later and usually by less.

reset: Within days of a Fed move
note: Credit cards and home equity lines are priced off the bank prime rate, which has sat 3 points above the target range's upper bound.
A fixed-rate mortgage does not change with the Fed. New mortgage rates follow longer-term bond yields rather than the target directly.
Euribor moves on expectations for ECB policy, so it often shifts before the decision itself.

reset: At the end of the fixed period
note: Germany and France lean fixed; Spain, Portugal and Finland lean variable.

reset: Usually from the next monthly payment
note: A tracker follows Bank Rate one for one.

benchmark: Fixed for two to five years
note: Most UK borrowers are on fixed deals and feel Bank Rate when they remortgage.
On many variable mortgages the payment stays fixed and the share going to interest changes instead.

benchmark: Fixed for the term, often five years
note: Fixed terms reprice when they renew.
Most Australian home loans are variable, one of the most direct channels to household budgets.

benchmark: Fixed for one to five years
reset: Rolls to variable when the fix ends
note: Fixed loans meet the cash rate when they roll off.
Overdrafts, floating loans and CDB yields move closely with the Selic.

benchmark: Often TR or IPCA plus a spread
note: Many home loans follow other indices, so mortgage pass-through is weaker.
